_note: Spoken guide scripts, one per destination slug. Recorded English lives in media/audio/guide-<slug>.mp3, other languages in guide_scripts.<lang>.json and guide-<slug>.<lang>.mp3. voice_guides.py records in the site voice, Jason, and re-records when the voice or the words change. Every English guide runs at least three minutes of speech, about five hundred words, and voice_guides.py refuses to record one shorter. Write for the ear: short sentences, concrete detail, one thing worth remembering and one thing to do. Numbers are spelled out because the reader says digits badly, and no long dashes.
pike-place-market:
Pike Place Market. This is the oldest continuously running farmers market in the country, open since nineteen oh seven, and it started as a protest. Onion prices had jumped tenfold in a season, so the city gave farmers a strip of planking above the waterfront and told them to sell straight to the public, no middleman. That rule survives. Almost every stall you pass is still the person who grew it, caught it, baked it or made it, which is why the prices make sense and the answers do too. Ask the woman with the peaches where they came from and she will name the orchard and the week. None of it is an act. The person selling is usually the person responsible, and they would rather tell you the truth than make the sale.

Come in under the big clock and the neon sign, because that is the picture in your head and it is worth having it match. Then keep going. The fish throwers at the corner counter are the show everybody films, and it is worth watching once. You will hear the whole crowd call the order back before you see the fish leave one man's hands and land in another's. Watch it, laugh, and then walk away from it, because the market is nine acres and four levels deep, and almost nobody goes down.

Under the main arcade there are magic shops, map dealers, a tiny record store and the old comic stall, and the crowds thin with every staircase you take. This is the part most people miss entirely. It is quieter down there, the light is low and yellow, and you can actually hear yourself think. Some of the windows on the lower levels open straight onto the bay, so you catch the grey light off the water between the shelves. Take your time. Follow a staircase just to see where it goes, and let yourself get a little lost, because getting lost is how you find the good corners.

Above ground it is a place for the nose as much as the eyes. Cut flowers by the armful, fish on ice, doughnuts frying, coffee, and the salt off the water underneath all of it. Produce is stacked in walls of colour, tomatoes and peppers and apples lined up like they are competing, and the people behind the tables will hand you a slice to try before you commit. The first Starbucks is across the cobbles at nineteen twelve Pike Place, and the line is usually forty minutes for coffee you can buy anywhere. Your call. If you only want the photograph of the sign, take it from across the street and keep walking.

One practical thing. Come before ten in the morning if you want photographs and flowers, come at noon if you want to eat, and do not come by car. The garage below fills by nine thirty on a weekend and the hill back up is steeper than it looks, so arrive on foot and save your legs for the stalls. Give this place two hours. It will take three, and the best hour will be one you did not plan. Buy something small from someone who made it, and eat it standing up looking at the water.
the-met-museum:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Five thousand years of human making under one roof on the edge of Central Park, and the honest advice comes first: nobody sees it all. Two million objects, two million square feet. Visitors who try to walk everything leave exhausted and remember nothing. Pick two wings and walk them slowly. That is the whole strategy, and the people who follow it have a better day than the people racing a map.

If you take one thing, take the Temple of Dendur. It is a real Egyptian temple, two thousand years old, that stood on the bank of the Nile until the Aswan dam was built and the water was going to swallow it. Egypt gave it to the United States for helping to rescue the monuments, and it was shipped here in six hundred and sixty one crates and rebuilt stone by stone in a hall of glass facing the park. Go right up to the wall and look for the old scratched names travellers left in the sandstone long ago. In the late afternoon the light comes across the reflecting pool and hits stone that was quarried before Rome. Stand there for a minute and let the room be quiet around you. It is the kind of room that makes people lower their voices without being told to.

Then wander. The American Wing courtyard is the quietest good room in the building, a place to sit down when your feet start to complain. The arms and armour hall is the one children never want to leave, full of horses in steel and swords taller than they are. And in summer the roof garden is open with a skyline view that most visitors never find, because it is not on the way to anything. That is exactly why you should go. The crowd is downstairs, and you are up in the trees looking at the park. Bring a bottle of water and wear shoes you can walk a marble floor in for hours, because the floors are hard and the building is long.

Here is the rhythm that works. Do not try to read every label. Let your eye pull you toward whatever it wants, walk to that, and only then read what it is. A museum this size punishes a straight line and rewards a wander. When you tire, sit. There are benches in nearly every gallery, and the objects are not going anywhere. Ten minutes of really looking at one painting beats an hour of glancing at fifty.

Two practical notes. The admission price is a suggestion for New York State residents and students from three neighbouring states, and a fixed ticket for everyone else, so have that ready before you reach the desk. And the Fifth Avenue steps are the meeting point for the whole city, which means if you get separated, that is where you go. Sit on them on the way out and watch the street for a while. Give it three hours and it will still be the fastest three hours of the trip. Pick your two wings before you walk in, and let everything else be a happy accident.
staten-island-ferry:
The Staten Island Ferry. This is the best free thing in New York and it is not close. Twenty five minutes across the harbour, no ticket, no booking, running twenty four hours a day, every day of the year, because it is not a tour. It is the commute. Thirty five thousand people ride it to work, which is exactly why it is still free and still frequent. You are getting a working boat, not a souvenir, and that is the charm of it. There is no line to buy a ticket because there is no ticket. You walk on, find a spot, and the harbour does the rest.

You leave from Whitehall Terminal at the bottom of Manhattan. Get there a few minutes early, watch for the gates to open, and walk on with everyone else. As the boat pulls out you get the whole financial district skyline pulling away behind you, then Governors Island, then the Statue of Liberty about a quarter mile off the starboard side, close enough to see her face, followed by Ellis Island where twelve million people entered this country. It is a lot of history for a ride that costs you nothing. Keep your eyes on the water and you will pass tugs, container ships and the odd sailboat, all of it going about its business around you.

Here is the part most visitors get wrong. Stand on the right hand side going out toward Staten Island, which is the starboard side, for the statue. Get there early and hold your spot at the rail, because everyone works this out eventually and the good side fills up. Coming back, stand at the front for the skyline, because the return run into Manhattan at dusk with the towers lighting up is the shot everybody wants, and half of them are facing the wrong way. If you only care about one direction, make it the trip home.

Go outside. The seats indoors are warm and the windows are scratched and salted, and you did not come across the harbour to look through smeared glass. The deck is where the wind is, where the gulls hang off the back of the boat, and where the light is honest. Stay out there the whole way if you can stand the cold. On a warm evening the deck is the best seat in the harbour, and it is still free.

At the far end you must get off the boat and walk back around through the terminal to reboard. It takes about five minutes and it is signposted, but if you stay in your seat you will be asked to leave anyway, so just go with it. There is a place to sit in the terminal if you need a minute before the next boat. The boats come often enough that a missed one is no disaster. Budget an hour and a quarter door to door and bring something warm. That harbour wind does not care what the forecast said. Ride out for the statue and ride back for the skyline, and let the free boat hand you the most expensive view in the city.
space-needle:
The Space Needle. Six hundred and five feet, built in about four hundred days for the nineteen sixty two World's Fair, and the whole thing began as a sketch on a napkin in a coffee house. The designer wanted a tethered balloon. The committee wanted a flying saucer. What you are looking at is the argument they settled on, and it has aged better than either idea deserved.

The foundation is the part worth knowing. They dug a hole thirty feet deep and poured four hundred and sixty seven concrete trucks in a single continuous day, the largest pour in the West at the time, and the foundation now weighs about the same as the tower standing on it. That is why it does not move much. It is built to take a wind of two hundred miles an hour and an earthquake of nine point one, and it has ridden out everything the region has thrown at it since. Stand at the base and look straight up the legs before you go in. The legs are wider than they look from a distance, and standing between them you get a sense of how much steel it takes to hold that saucer in the sky. From directly underneath it looks less like a saucer and more like something about to take off.

Up top the observation deck was rebuilt with floor to ceiling glass and open air glass benches that lean you out over the drop. Sit on one if your stomach allows it. The floor below is the Loupe, the world's only revolving glass floor. It turns slowly enough that you notice it only when you look down and the city has moved, and there is a particular pleasure in watching someone realise the ground under their feet is quietly turning. It is a small strange thrill, and worth the wait for a clear patch of glass.

Walk the whole deck, do not just pick one side. Each face of the tower gives you a different city. One way is the water and the ferries, another is downtown stacked up close, another is the mountains if the day is kind. Give it a full slow lap. And go out into the open air section, because the wind and the sound of the city coming up at you is the thing you will remember long after the photographs.

One honest piece of advice. This is a clear day attraction. On a grey Seattle afternoon you are paying to stand inside a cloud, and the cloud looks the same from the ground for free. Check the mountain first. If you can see Rainier from the street, go up now, because the weather here turns without warning and a clear hour is not a promise. If you cannot, spend the money at Chihuly next door and come back tomorrow. And book a timed ticket, because the walk up queue on a sunny weekend runs past an hour, and an hour in line is an hour you could have spent up in the air. Pick your moment, go up while it is clear, and take one slow lap before you look at your phone.
bainbridge-island-ferry:
The Bainbridge Island ferry. Thirty five minutes each way across Puget Sound, and it is the cheapest good hour in Seattle. You pay only going west, walk on for a few dollars, and the ride home is free, so a round trip costs you one fare and about ninety minutes. For that you get a full crossing of the sound and back, which is a bargain by any measure. Buy your ticket at the counter or the machines inside the terminal, then follow the crowd down to the boat.

Go up to the outside deck as soon as you board and stay there. The seats inside are fine and warm and everybody uses them, but the whole reason to take this boat is the part you can only see from the rail. Leaving Colman Dock you get the downtown skyline stacked against the hills with the Space Needle off to the right, and on a clear day Mount Rainier standing behind the whole city looking close enough to touch, which it is not. It is sixty miles away and fourteen thousand feet tall. That is the thing locals mean when they say the mountain is out. Look ahead and the Olympic range fills the far shore.

This is a working ferry, one of the busiest in the country, carrying islanders with groceries and dogs and bicycles, so it runs in fog and it runs in rain. The rain does not stop it and it should not stop you. Wet weather on this crossing has its own quality, with the islands going soft and grey and the gulls riding the wake right at the rail. Bring a jacket and stand out in it. The deck clears when it drizzles, which means you get the rail to yourself, and the water on a grey day is its own kind of beautiful. You will be sharing the rail with people who do this every day and barely look up, which is its own quiet lesson in what a view is worth.

Watch the wake, watch the birds, and watch the other boats. This is a real shipping lane, so you may see a container ship, a sailboat, or a smaller ferry crossing the other way. It is a working sound doing its work, and you have a front row seat for the price of a cup of coffee.

At the far end, Winslow is a ten minute walk up from the dock, a single main street with a good bookshop, a bakery, and a handful of places to eat looking back at the water. Give yourself an hour there and catch the boat back at sunset, when the light goes gold behind the city and the skyline you sailed away from comes back to meet you. One thing that will save your evening. Check the sailing time before you walk up into town. Miss it and the next one can be an hour, which is a long time to stand on a dock watching the boat you wanted pull away. Stand at the rail on the ride home and let the city grow back up in front of you.
lincoln-memorial:
The Lincoln Memorial. Approach it on foot from the reflecting pool if you can, because the building was made to be walked up to, not driven past. It sits at the far west end of the National Mall, and the climb up the steps is part of the point. Give yourself the long approach and let the figure inside grow as you rise toward it.

Thirty six columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died, and the man himself sitting nineteen feet high in Georgia marble. The sculptor Daniel Chester French worked on it for four years. As you come through the columns the figure is in shadow at first, then fills the whole far wall as you get close. Look at the hands. The left is clenched, the right is open and relaxed, and people have argued for a century about whether he carved the letters A and L in sign language into them. The family always said no. Visitors keep seeing it anyway. Then look at the face, which was carved to be read from below and changes with the light. Stand a moment and let your eyes adjust, because the chamber is dim on purpose, and the marble looks different once they do.

Read the walls, because the walls are the memorial. On the south side is the Gettysburg Address, two hundred and seventy two words that took about two minutes to deliver and that the newspapers of the day called a failure. On the north is the Second Inaugural, given one month before he was killed, with the line about malice toward none and charity for all carved where anyone can stand and read it. Read them slowly. They were written to be heard out loud, and they still work that way.

Then turn around and find the spot on the steps. Eighteen steps down from the chamber there is an inscription in the stone marking where Martin Luther King junior stood on the twenty eighth of August nineteen sixty three and told a quarter of a million people about a dream, with Lincoln directly behind him. It is a small engraved line and most people walk over it. Look for it before you look at the view, because once you have stood on it, the view means more. From there the Mall runs east in a straight line, the pool at your feet and the monument beyond.

Come at night if you can. The memorial never closes, it is lit from within, the crowds are gone, and the reflecting pool holds the Washington Monument upside down all the way to the far end. The marble goes warm and gold under the lights, and the sound drops to almost nothing. If daytime is your only window, come early, before the tour buses, and you will get some of the same quiet. Twenty minutes here is enough. Spend one of them just standing at the top of the steps with your back to the statue, looking east the way he does. It will stay with you longer than that.
empire-state-building:
The Empire State Building. You will see it long before you reach it, so let the walk in be part of the visit, and look straight up from the sidewalk on Fifth Avenue before you ever go inside. One thousand four hundred and fifty four feet to the tip, built in one year and forty five days during the Great Depression, at a pace of about four and a half floors a week. Three thousand four hundred workers, many of them Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake who walked the beams without harnesses, hundreds of feet up, eating lunch on girders over open air. It came in ahead of schedule and under budget, which has essentially never happened since, and it is worth pausing on the sidewalk to take in the whole height of it before your neck gives out.

It opened in nineteen thirty one to an empty city. Nobody could afford the offices, so New Yorkers called it the Empty State Building for years, and it survived on ticket money from people paying to go up. The observatory kept it alive. In nineteen forty five a B twenty five bomber lost in fog flew into the seventy ninth floor. Fourteen people died, and the building was open for business again on Monday. Keep that in mind on the way up. The lobby with its ceiling of steel and gold, and the elevator ride itself, carry more history than most towers you will ever stand in, so do not rush the parts before the view. Give the ground floor a slow look before you queue.

There are two decks. The eighty sixth is the one you want, outdoors, open air, with the wind and the sound of the city coming up at you. Stand at the railing and you will hear traffic, sirens and horns rising all the way from the street, thinned out and strange at that height. Walk all four sides, because each one is a different city. The hundred and second is glassed in, higher, and costs more, and on most days it does not give you enough extra to be worth it. Save your money and spend the time outside instead.

Timing decides everything here. Sunset is the most crowded hour of the day, and the line for the railing can eat the whole view. Go at eight in the morning when it opens and you will share it with almost nobody, or go after ten at night when the last families have gone and the grid below is fully lit. Dress warmer than the street, because the wind up there has a bite the sidewalk does not. Book a timed ticket either way, and go straight for the open air deck first while it is quiet, then look around inside on your way back down.

Know that the tower lights change colour for holidays and causes, so whatever colour it is tonight, it means something. When you come down, cross the street, find a corner with a clear line up, and look at the top one more time. You have just been standing where that light is, higher than almost everything around it. That is the thing to carry home.
central-park:
Central Park. Eight hundred and forty three acres in the middle of Manhattan, and none of it is natural. Every hill, lake, meadow and outcrop was designed and built by hand between eighteen fifty seven and eighteen seventy six. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux moved nearly three million cubic yards of soil and rock and planted something like four million trees and shrubs on what had been swamp and stone. It is one of the largest works of landscape art in the world, and it is pretending to be a place that just happened. Once you know that, you start to see the design everywhere, and the park gets better for it.

Look for the four transverse roads that carry traffic across the park. Olmsted sank them below the sight lines so a crosstown bus would never interrupt the view from a footpath. That single decision is why the park still feels like countryside a hundred and fifty years later. Stand on a rise and listen. You will hear birds and footsteps and almost no engines, in the middle of one of the loudest cities on earth. That quiet is engineered, and it took twenty years to build. When you notice the towers over the treeline, that is the design too, the wild framing the city instead of the other way round.

If you have one hour, walk the Mall under the elms, cross Bethesda Terrace to the fountain, and go up to Bow Bridge. That is the postcard, and it earns it. Come down the stairs at the terrace slowly and look up at the tiled ceiling underneath, which most people rush straight past. If you have two hours, add the Ramble behind the lake, thirty six acres of deliberately confusing woodland where people go to get lost on purpose and where the birdwatchers gather during migration. Go slow in there, and let yourself take a wrong turn or two.

Practical points. The park is bigger than it looks on a map, over two and a half miles top to bottom, so pick a gate and a direction rather than trying to cross the whole thing. Wear shoes you can walk in for hours, because you will walk further than you plan to. The lamp posts have four digit numbers on them: the first two digits are the nearest street, which is how you find yourself when you are lost. Learn that trick before you need it, and you will never be truly lost in here.

And it is free, always, all of it. There is no gate, no ticket and no closing whistle for the grounds themselves, and no two visits look the same, because the light and the season keep changing the place. Before you leave, pick one bench, sit for ten minutes, and watch the city use its own back garden. Runners, prams, chess players, a saxophone somewhere under the trees, someone asleep in the sun. That is the park doing exactly what it was built to do, a hundred and fifty years on, and it is the thing to take with you when you walk back out into the traffic.
brooklyn-bridge:
The Brooklyn Bridge. Opened in eighteen eighty three, the first steel wire suspension bridge in the world, and for twenty years the longest span on earth. It cost fifteen million dollars and at least twenty seven lives, and the story of who finished it is the reason to walk it, not just to cross it. Start on the Brooklyn side, near the top of the ramp, and give yourself a minute before you step on. The wooden walkway runs above the traffic, so you are up in the cables the whole way over, and the boards give a little under your feet.

It cost more than money. John Roebling designed it and died of tetanus before construction began, after a ferry crushed his foot while he was surveying the site. His son Washington took over and was paralysed by decompression sickness from working in the pressurised caissons dug into the riverbed. So Emily Roebling, Washington's wife, learned the mathematics, the cable specifications and the engineering, and ran the project for eleven years, carrying her husband's instructions to the site while he watched through a telescope from their window in Brooklyn Heights. She was the first person to cross it. Carry that with you as you walk, because you are walking on her work.

The public did not trust it. Six days after it opened, a rumour that it was collapsing caused a stampede that killed twelve people. So the next year P T Barnum walked twenty one elephants across it, and that settled the argument. Look up at the two stone towers as you pass beneath them, and follow the cables with your eye where they cross into the diagonal stays. They were among the tallest things in the city when they went up, and people came just to stand under them, the way you are doing now.

Walk it from Brooklyn toward Manhattan, not the other way. That direction puts the skyline in front of you the whole crossing instead of behind your shoulder, growing taller with every step. It is about a mile and takes thirty to forty minutes with stops. Stop in the middle, at the first tower, and look down through the cables at the water and the ferries below. That is the spot most people remember afterward, so let yourself linger there rather than pushing straight on. You will feel the deck move a little under the traffic, and that is normal.

Stay in the pedestrian lane and out of the bike lane, because those cyclists are commuting and they are fast, and the line between the two lanes is the one rule the bridge really enforces. Early morning light is the good light, and it is also the only hour the walkway is not shoulder to shoulder. Come at dawn if you can stand the early start. You will have the cables, the towers and the harbour close to yourself, the gulls and the wind off the water for company, and the city will be waking up in front of you the whole way across. Walk slowly. This one is worth the extra ten minutes.
9-11-memorial-and-museum:
The National September Eleventh Memorial. Come to it quietly, and give yourself a little time before you arrive to slow down. Two square voids set exactly in the footprints of the towers that stood here, each an acre, with water falling thirty feet down all four sides into a second, smaller void at the centre that you cannot see the bottom of. The architect Michael Arad called the design Reflecting Absence, and the point is that the emptiness is kept, not filled. Stand at the edge and watch the water go over. The sound of it covers the city behind you, which is part of the design, and the further into the plaza you walk the more the noise of the streets falls away.

The names of two thousand nine hundred and seventy seven people killed here, at the Pentagon, in Shanksville, and in the nineteen ninety three bombing are cut through the bronze parapets. Run your hand along them if you feel moved to. They are not alphabetical. They are arranged by what the memorial calls meaningful adjacencies: colleagues beside colleagues, first responders beside their companies, friends beside friends, from requests the families made. People who died together are together. Take the time to read a few of the names slowly, rather than passing them all in a blur. The bronze warms in the sun and stays cool in shade, so the letters feel different depending on where the light is.

Look for the Survivor Tree on the plaza. A Callery pear pulled from the rubble in October two thousand and one, eight feet of burned trunk with one living branch. It was nursed back in a Bronx nursery for nine years and replanted here. It is now taller than the buildings around the plaza edge, and every spring it flowers before the other trees. It is easy to walk past among the others, so look for the one with slightly different bark and a small marker at its base.

The plaza is free and open, and it is a working part of the city, with office workers crossing it and children on the grass, which is part of what it means. The museum below is ticketed and takes two hours and it is heavy, so decide honestly whether you want that today. There is no wrong answer. Some people come only to the pools and leave, and that is a complete visit. If you do go down, go when you are rested, not at the end of a long day, because it asks a great deal of you.

Whichever you choose, this is a burial ground for many of the people named here. Speak quietly. Keep your voice low, put your phone away at the parapets, and let other people have their moment at the names they came to find. On a birthday the staff place a white rose in that person's name. If you see one tucked into the bronze, you are looking at someone's birthday. Stand with it a moment before you go, and then leave the way you came, quietly.
grand-central-terminal:
Grand Central Terminal. Not station, terminal, because the tracks end here. Forty four platforms and sixty seven tracks on two levels, the most of any railway station in the world, all of it buried under the street so that Park Avenue could be built on top. That was the deal that paid for the building in nineteen thirteen: bury the trains, sell the air. Come in off the street and give yourself a second to adjust. It is loud, it is fast, and everyone but you seems to know exactly where they are going. Let them. You are not here to catch a train.

Walk into the middle of the main concourse and stop. People will flow around you like water around a rock, which is fine, because you need to look up. The ceiling is the night sky, twenty five hundred stars, sixty of them lit, and it is backwards. The constellations are reversed, as if you were looking down at the sky from outside it rather than up from the ground. The official explanation is that it was painted from a medieval manuscript that showed the heavens from God's point of view. The likelier explanation is that somebody flipped the drawing. The family who commissioned it declined to fix it, and so the mistake is a hundred years old now and beloved.

Look for one small dark rectangle near the crab of Cancer. That is the original grime, left uncleaned in the nineteen nineties restoration so visitors could see what decades of tobacco smoke had done to the whole ceiling. The rest of the vault is that soft green because someone scrubbed it. That one patch is what the entire room used to look like. It is easy to miss, so find the crab first and the dirt is right beside it.

Then go find the whisper. Head down the ramp toward the Oyster Bar and look for the four low arches outside the door, a shallow vault of pale tile. Stand facing into one corner while a friend faces into the opposite corner, twenty feet away, and speak in a low voice straight at the tile. The vault carries your words up and across to them and to nobody standing in between. It works every time, it costs nothing, and half the people walking past have no idea it is there. Try it once with something silly and you will understand why couples get engaged in that corner.

A few plain things. The concourse is busiest at the morning and evening rush, when the whole floor becomes a river, so if you want photographs come mid morning or mid afternoon, when the light comes through the tall east windows and the crowd has thinned. The information booth in the centre, the one with the four faced brass clock on top, is the meeting spot the whole city uses, so if you get separated, that is where you go. Before you leave, stand still one more time and just listen to the sound of ten thousand footsteps moving under a painted sky. Then walk out into the city knowing you saw the ceiling that nobody ever looks up at.
the-high-line:
The High Line. A mile and a half of freight railway thirty feet above the West Side, built in the nineteen thirties to get trains off the street after so many people were killed at level crossings that Tenth Avenue was called Death Avenue. The last train ran in nineteen eighty carrying three carloads of frozen turkeys, and then the line sat abandoned for twenty five years while the property owners below tried to have it torn down. What saved it was that it had gone wild. Seeds blew in, and a self sown meadow of grasses and birch grew up in the ballast between the rails, thirty feet in the air, in the middle of Manhattan.

A photographer spent a year documenting that accidental meadow, two neighbours founded a group to protect it, and the planting you walk through today is a deliberate echo of what grew here on its own, with about half the species native to the region. That is the thing to hold in your head as you go. This looks like a garden and it is one, but it is a garden imitating a happy accident, laid on top of the steel a train used to run on. Look down between the plants and you can still see the old rails, left in place, running through the beds.

Walk it from Gansevoort Street at the south end and go north, which is the way the story unfolds. You pass through buildings, not just between them, close enough to see into the windows, and the section at Tenth Avenue drops you into a sunken amphitheatre with a big pane of glass looking straight down the avenue at the traffic below. Sit there for a few minutes. It is the best free seat in the neighbourhood, and watching the cars stack up at the light through that window is oddly satisfying, like the city is putting on a show it does not know about.

Notice how the sound changes as you climb up out of the streets. Down at ground level it is horns and engines, and up here it drops away to footsteps and wind in the grasses and, in the warm months, bees. The planting shifts with the seasons, so what you see depends on the month you come, tall and gold in autumn, bare and architectural in winter, green and loose in high summer.

A few practical things. It is a linear park, so there are limited entrances and most of them have stairs, with lifts at Gansevoort, Fourteenth, Twenty third and Thirtieth if you need one. Budget forty five minutes to walk it end to end without stopping, and more like ninety with the stopping you will actually do. And pick your hour. Go early in the morning or at dusk, because the middle of a summer afternoon up there is a slow moving queue of people with no shade to duck into, and the quiet and the space, which are the whole point, get trampled flat. Walk the length of it once without your phone out, and let the old railway show you the backs of the buildings that the city usually keeps to itself.
times-square:
Times Square. Let us be honest about what this is. It is an advertising space that became a landmark, and roughly three hundred and thirty thousand people pass through it every day. New Yorkers avoid it, and they are not wrong to. You should still see it once, at night, for about twenty minutes, because there is nothing else quite like standing inside that much light.

It was Longacre Square, the carriage trade district, until the New York Times moved its headquarters here in nineteen oh four and the city renamed it after the paper. The Times celebrated with a fireworks display on New Year's Eve, and when fireworks were later banned they lowered an illuminated ball down the flagpole instead. That was nineteen oh seven. It has happened almost every year since, and it is why a million people stand out here in the cold each December, waiting for a ball to slide down a pole.

The square has not always looked like this. By the nineteen seventies it had become the most dangerous block in the city, and the cleanup that followed was so complete that the zoning now legally requires the illuminated signs. Every landlord on the square must maintain a certain brightness. Think about that for a second. The glare is not an accident and it is not only commerce, it is written into the law, and at night the light is strong enough to read a newspaper by at one in the morning. Stand in the middle of it and look up, and you are looking at a building code.

Here is how to actually enjoy it. Come after dark, because the lights are the whole event and in daylight this is just a crowded intersection. Find the red steps above the TKTS booth at the north end, the glowing staircase that goes nowhere, and sit down. They are free, nobody moves you along, and they face south into the full wall of screens, which is the best view in the square. Give it twenty minutes of sitting and watching the light change and the crowd churn. The screens never repeat for long, and the whole square seems to breathe, brightening and dimming as the ads cycle, so it never quite settles into one picture.

Now the warnings, and take these seriously. The costumed characters, the cartoon mascots and the painted people, are not employees of anyone, and they will ask you for money after the photograph is taken, sometimes firmly. Agree the price before you pose, or simply do not pose. The same spirit applies to the restaurants right on the square. They are the worst value in the city, trading entirely on their address, so walk one street away in any direction and your food gets better and cheaper immediately. That is the trick to this place. Do not fight it and do not try to love it. Treat it like a firework, something loud and bright and brief. See it blaze once at night, feel how strange it is to stand in what looks like daylight at midnight, and then turn a corner and let the real city close back over your head.
chihuly-garden-and-glass:
Chihuly Garden and Glass. Dale Chihuly grew up in Tacoma, an hour south of here, and he changed what glass could be. This is the permanent collection at the foot of the Space Needle, eight galleries, a glasshouse, and a garden, and it is the rare attraction that is better in bad weather, so save it for the grey day the forecast is promising you.

Move through the indoor galleries slowly, because the light is doing the work and it rewards standing still. The rooms are kept dark and the glass is lit from within, so the colour seems to come from inside the objects rather than land on them. Then you reach the centrepiece, the Glasshouse, a hundred foot long room under a curved glass roof, with a suspended sculpture forty three feet long in reds, oranges and yellows hanging overhead. When the Seattle sky is flat grey, and it often is, that river of warm colour against the cloud is the entire point. Sit down on one of the benches, lean your head back, and give it a few minutes. This is the room to linger in.

Outside in the garden the glass forms are planted right among the real plants, spears and orbs and reeds pushed up between the flowers, so that you keep having to look twice to work out which is living and which is blown. When it rains, and it will, the pieces bead with water and get better, the drops catching light along every curve. Most people rush the garden to get back inside. Do the opposite.

The man behind all this has a story worth carrying around with you. Chihuly lost the sight in his left eye in a car accident in nineteen seventy six, and dislocated a shoulder bodysurfing three years later, so he stopped blowing the glass himself. He directs teams now. He once described it as being more choreographer than dancer, and here is the strange part: the work got larger and more ambitious after he stopped holding the pipe, not smaller. Standing under a sculpture the length of a bus, made by a man who cannot do the blowing himself, is a quiet argument about what it takes to make something.

A few practical notes. It takes about an hour to walk through, a little more if you sit in the Glasshouse, which you should. Combined tickets with the Space Needle next door cost less than buying the two separately, so if the day is clear enough to do both, buy them together. And this is the real reason to keep it in your pocket. If the mountain is hidden and the sky is low and going up the Needle would just be paying to stand inside a cloud, this is the answer. It is indoors, it is fifty yards away, and the weather cannot touch it. So watch the sky for a day when Seattle turns the colour of a dishcloth, and come here then. Stand under the glass, look up, and let the room hand you back the colour that the weather took away.
gas-works-park:
Gas Works Park. This was a coal gasification plant that ran from nineteen oh six to nineteen fifty six, making the gas that lit Seattle's streetlamps, and when it closed the site was a poisoned twenty acre ruin sitting on the best waterfront in the city. Everyone assumed the towers would come down. Nobody in nineteen seventy thought a family would ever spread a picnic blanket in the shadow of a dead gas plant.

The landscape architect Richard Haag spent months on the site and argued the opposite of what everyone expected. Keep the machinery. It was a genuinely radical idea at the time, that industrial wreckage could be beautiful rather than shameful, and the city fought him on it. He won. The cracking towers still stand, rusted and enormous, at the north end, fenced off but right there, and the old exhauster compressor building was painted in bright colours and turned into a play barn where children climb the actual machines. Walk up to the towers first. They are bigger than photographs suggest, and there is something about a rusted industrial cathedral left standing in a park that a new sculpture could never buy.

Haag also pioneered the cleanup. Rather than digging out all the contaminated ground and hauling it away, he used bioremediation, seeding the soil with organisms to digest the hydrocarbons in place. It was one of the first uses of that approach anywhere, and it is standard practice now. So the grass you are sitting on was cleaned by the ground itself, slowly, from the inside. It is worth knowing, and it is also the reason there are still spots where you are asked to stay on the path.

Now climb the Great Mound, the grass hill at the water's edge. It is a short pull and the whole point of the park is at the top. Set into the summit there is a bronze and concrete sundial that uses your own shadow as the pointer, so you stand on the marked spot, look down, and read the time off your own body. Children love it, and adults are quietly delighted the first time it actually works. From up there you get the full downtown skyline straight across Lake Union, with float planes dropping down onto the water in front of it, engines buzzing, and sailboats crossing underneath. On a clear evening the light comes low across the lake and the whole city goes gold.

This is the best free view in Seattle, and it is also a working neighbourhood park, so you will be sharing the hill with dogs, kites, and people eating dinner out of paper bags. On the fourth of July it is the place the whole city goes, and the mound fills shoulder to shoulder for the fireworks over the lake. The rest of the year it is calm. Bring something to sit on and come toward the end of the day. Climb the mound, stand on the marked spot until your shadow tells you the hour, and then just watch the float planes come down over a skyline that a poisoned ruin turned out to be the best seat for.
kerry-park-viewpoint:
Kerry Park. Do not expect much of the place itself. This is a strip of pavement and grass about the size of a tennis court, wedged onto a hillside street, and it is the single most photographed spot in Seattle. Every postcard you have seen, every establishing shot in every film set in this city, was taken from roughly where you are standing now. You arrive, you turn to face the water, and the whole thing does its work in about ten seconds. It was given to the city in nineteen twenty seven by Albert and Katharine Kerry, so that, in their words, all who stop here may enjoy this view. That is the entire mission of the park, and it still holds. There is no cafe, no gift shop, no visitor centre. There is a low stone wall, a piece of sculpture, and the view.

The reason the view works is the composition, and it is worth taking a moment to actually read it rather than just raising your phone. The Space Needle sits in the middle distance at exactly the right height, neither lost below you nor towering over you. Downtown stacks up behind it in a bank of towers. Elliott Bay runs across the bottom of the frame, usually with a ferry or a container ship crossing it slowly. And on a clear day Mount Rainier floats above the whole thing to the south, sixty miles away and looking like a matte painting somebody hung there. Nothing else in the city lines all four of those up at once.

Here is the timing that matters. Come at dusk, about twenty minutes after sunset, when the sky still has some colour left in it and the office towers have switched their lights on. The sky goes deep blue, the windows go gold, and the Needle lights up in the middle of it. That is the twenty minute window everybody comes for, which means you will be sharing the wall with a row of tripods and a lot of quiet elbowing for position. Be gracious about it, and get there early enough to claim a spot. If you would rather have the place to yourself, come at sunrise instead. It is nearly empty, though the light then comes from behind the city, which is harder to photograph and easier to just stand and enjoy.

Two practical things before you go. This is a residential street on the south slope of Queen Anne, with almost no parking and neighbours who have lived with the crowds outside their windows for decades. Circle for a space, do not block driveways, and keep your voice down after dark. And understand what you are here for. There is nothing at Kerry Park but the view. Ten minutes is the whole visit, so do not build an afternoon around it. Pair it with a walk on the hill, or a coffee up in the Queen Anne shops, and treat this as the one perfect stop in between.

So stand at the wall, put the phone down for the first minute, and just watch the light change. The photograph will still be there when you pick it back up.
museum-of-pop-culture:
The Museum of Pop Culture, MoPOP. You will have opinions about the building before you ever reach the door, so let us start there. Frank Gehry designed it, and he began the way few architects would admit to. He bought several Fender Stratocasters, cut them apart, and used the broken pieces as the model for the shape. What grew out of that is a skin of twenty one thousand shingles in gold, silver, red, blue and purple, no two curved panels the same. People have called it a smashed guitar, and worse. Walk all the way around it before you go in. The colour shifts as the light moves and as you move, and the monorail runs straight through the middle of the thing, which never stops being strange.

Paul Allen founded it, and it started as a shrine to one man. Jimi Hendrix was from Seattle, and Allen's collection of his instruments and his handwritten lyrics is the seed the whole museum grew around. Stand close to the lyric sheets. Seeing a song you know in someone's actual handwriting, with the crossings out and the second thoughts, does something a printed page never will. From Hendrix the story widens into the music this city is most famous for. Nirvana came next, then the whole grunge story, told in the place that made it. There are Kurt Cobain's guitars, and the flyers pulled off the telephone poles, the cheap photocopied ones that advertised shows in rooms that held a hundred people. It is a reminder that all of it started small and local, in bars a short drive from where you are standing.

The museum has since widened well beyond music, into science fiction, horror and fantasy, and that is where it gets fun. There are original props, costumes and manuscripts, the real things from films and books you grew up with. The horror gallery is genuinely effective in the dark, so if you scare easily, take that as fair warning rather than a dare. Give yourself time to read the cases and not just glance at them, because the labels here are better than most.

Then go upstairs to the Sound Lab, which is the part most people miss and the part you will remember. It gives you real instruments in soundproof rooms with nobody watching. You can pick up a drum kit or a guitar and be genuinely terrible in private, for as long as you like, and no one outside the glass can hear a note. Even if you have never held an instrument, go in, shut the door, and hit something. That is the whole point. Give it two hours, and do not feel you have to rush. It is entirely indoors, which on a grey Seattle day is the quiet superpower of this place. It sits right next to the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, and the three of them together will fill a full wet afternoon without asking you to be outside for more than a minute at a time.

So find the Sound Lab, close the door, and make some noise nobody has to hear. It is the one museum in town that dares you to be bad at something, and it means it.
seattle-aquarium:
The Seattle Aquarium, out on Pier fifty nine, sitting right over the water it studies. That is the thing that sets it apart from most aquariums, and it is worth knowing before you walk in. The animals here are largely from Puget Sound, which is a few hundred feet away, and the water in the tanks is pumped straight in from under the pier. What you are looking at did not come from the other side of the world. It came from just outside. Start at the Window on Washington Waters, a tank twenty feet wide holding eighteen thousand gallons of Neah Bay, with rockfish and salmon and anemones. Several times a day a diver climbs in and talks to you through a microphone from inside the water, answering whatever the crowd shouts, which is the best free show in the building. Time your visit to catch one if you can, and let the children stand at the front. From there you reach the Underwater Dome, a glass room with three hundred and sixty degrees of fish circling above you and all around you. Stand in the middle, look up, and give your eyes a moment to stop tracking any single fish. It is closer to floating than watching.

Then go and find the giant Pacific octopus, and do not rush past it. This is the largest octopus species in the world. It can span twenty feet, it has nine brains and three hearts, and roughly two thirds of its neurons live in its arms, so each arm partly thinks for itself. Watch one move and you can almost see that happening, an arm investigating a corner while the rest of the animal is busy elsewhere. They are also famous escape artists and problem solvers, which is exactly why the lids on their tanks are latched. Every year around Valentine's Day the aquarium introduces a male and a female in public and lets the city watch, which tells you how much personality people credit these animals with.

The sea otters are the crowd, and for good reason, but the story behind them is worth carrying past the glass. They were hunted to local extinction here for their fur, which is the densest of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch. The Washington population you are looking at today all descends from fifty nine animals relocated from Alaska in nineteen sixty nine. Every otter grooming itself in front of you is part of a comeback that very nearly did not happen. Watch how constantly they work at that fur. That density is the whole reason they are alive, and the whole reason they were nearly gone.

Ninety minutes covers the place comfortably, and it does not ask for a whole day. Wear something you do not mind getting a little damp near the touch pools, and go on the earlier side if you want the tanks to yourself before the school groups arrive. It is a short flat walk from Pike Place Market, so it pairs easily with a morning up in the stalls.

So find the octopus, stand still, and watch one arm make up its own mind. Nothing else in the building will make you rethink what an animal is quite so fast.
starbucks-reserve-roastery:
The Starbucks Reserve Roastery, up on Capitol Hill. Ignore the sign over the door for a moment, because that name will give you the wrong idea. What this really is, is a fifteen thousand square foot working coffee factory that you are allowed to wander around inside, and it happens to have bars in it. You do not come here for a paper cup to go. You come to stand inside the machine.

Walk to the middle first. The copper cask at the centre holds green coffee, the raw unroasted beans, and they get roasted on site in the drums you can see running along the wall. After roasting, the beans travel overhead through clear tubes to the bars, so you can genuinely stand there and watch your coffee move across the ceiling to the counter where it will be brewed. The whole room smells of it, warm and toasty and a little sweet, and the roasters are loud in a way that tells you this is real work and not a display. Look closely at the cask and you will see symbols stamped into the metal. They are a made up language that spells out the roasting process, which is either charming or a bit much, depending on your mood.

The reason to come, though, is what they brew here that no ordinary Starbucks does. There are single origin lots in small quantities, siphon vacuum brewers that look like chemistry glassware, cold brew poured off a nitrogen tap, and a machine called the Clover that brews one cup at a time under vacuum. This is where you should do the one thing almost nobody does. Ask the person behind the bar what came in this week and let them choose for you. They are trained to talk about this coffee at length and hardly anyone gives them the chance, so you will get their full attention and probably something you would never have picked yourself. The food is worth knowing about too. Princi bakes on site, so what you are eating is real and made that morning, not shipped in. And if you come in the evening, the upstairs bar serves coffee cocktails, which turns the place into something quite different after dark.

Now two honest notes, because this is not the corner shop. It is expensive, several times the price of the Starbucks you passed on the way here, so treat it as an experience you are buying rather than a quick caffeine stop. And it is busy, from mid morning until late, with lines that can swallow the whole main floor. The fix is simple. Go on a weekday before ten in the morning and you will have the roasting floor nearly to yourself, with time to watch the drums and actually talk to the staff. One more thing worth knowing before you set out. It is a fifteen minute walk uphill from downtown, and in Seattle that often means walking uphill in the rain, so dress for it.

So skip the drink you already know, lean on the bar, and ask them to surprise you. That is the only order in this building that uses the place for what it really is.
washington-monument:
The Washington Monument. Five hundred and fifty five feet of marble, the tallest stone structure in the world, and the first thing to do is look, not up, but about a third of the way up. You will see the stone change colour, a clear line running right around the shaft where one shade of marble gives way to another. That line is the whole story of this thing, so let me tell it. Construction began in eighteen forty eight, and it stopped in eighteen fifty four, when the money ran out and the political society that had seized control of the project stalled the whole thing. So the stump stood unfinished all through the Civil War, a hundred and fifty feet of abandoned masonry with cattle grazing at the base. Mark Twain looked at it and called it a factory chimney with the top broken off. For a generation it was less a monument than a national embarrassment, sitting half built on the most important lawn in the country.

Work finally restarted in eighteen seventy nine, twenty five years after it had stopped. By then the quarry that had supplied the original marble could no longer match it, so the builders used stone from elsewhere, and it never quite lined up. That is why the tower is two different stones, and always will be. Stand back far enough to see the seam and you are looking at the exact moment the country picked the project back up. It was finished in eighteen eighty four, and capped with a nine inch piece of aluminium, which sounds like nothing today. At the time aluminium was a precious metal, more expensive than silver, and the cap was displayed in a jewellery shop window before it was carried up and set on top.

Inside there is an elevator to the observation level at five hundred feet, with a window on each side of the shaft. Each one frames something. The Capitol lies to the east, the Lincoln Memorial to the west, the White House to the north, and the Jefferson Memorial to the south. It is the plan of the whole city laid out through four small windows, and it makes sense of the map in a way no map does.

Now the practical part, because it matters here. Tickets are free, but they are timed, and they go fast. They are released online at ten in the morning the day before, and the walk up queue for same day tickets is small, so your best bet is to book ahead the moment they drop. If you miss them, do not treat that as a failure. Plan instead to admire the monument from the grass, which is genuinely fine, and maybe better. Spread out on the lawn, look up at that colour change, and you have understood the thing without waiting in a single line.

And here is the quiet joke of the place. The best view in Washington, the one down the length of the Mall with everything lined up, does not include the monument at all. This tower you are standing under is the one landmark you cannot see from the finest view of the city. So climb it if you can, but if you cannot, lie back on the grass and enjoy being inside the one picture the postcard leaves out.
jefferson-memorial:
The Jefferson Memorial, across the Tidal Basin, and it is the one people skip because it is a walk. Take the walk. Most of the crowd stays on the north side of the water with the Lincoln Memorial and the monument, so the far shore is quieter almost by default, and the quiet is the point. You will hear the water before you reach the building, and the traffic thins the further round you go.

It is modelled on the Pantheon in Rome, which Jefferson admired and borrowed from for his own house at Monticello and for the rotunda at the University of Virginia, so the building is quoting the man's own taste back at him. Walk up the steps and stand under the dome before you look at anything else. The columns frame the water, the ceiling opens above you, and the whole room is built to make one figure feel larger than he was. The marble carries sound, so voices drop without anyone deciding to, and on a weekday morning you may have the round chamber almost to yourself, with only the shuffle of feet and the wind off the basin coming through the columns.

Inside, a nineteen foot bronze stands looking out across the water at the White House. Walk a slow circle around it and read the four panels on the walls, which are his words. The fourth is the one to read. Laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind, he wrote. As new discoveries are made, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times. It is an argument, carved in stone, against treating anything as finished. Stand with it a moment. Most people photograph the statue and miss the sentence.

The memorial was controversial when it was built in the nineteen thirties. Cherry trees had to be moved for it and women chained themselves to the trees in protest, which is why the planting around it is now so carefully protected. For two weeks each spring, those trees, a gift from Tokyo in nineteen twelve, turn the whole basin pink and this becomes the most crowded quarter mile in the city. If you come in those two weeks, come at first light or not at all, because by mid morning the path around the water is shoulder to shoulder and slow.

Come at sunrise if you can, any time of year. The light comes across the water straight into the columns, the joggers are the only company, and the reflection of the dome in the basin is the reason photographers set an alarm. Stand at the edge of the water on the near side and let the whole building hang upside down in it. It is about a twenty minute walk from the Lincoln Memorial around the water, and there is no closer parking, so plan the legs. Wear shoes you can walk in and bring water in summer, because there is little shade on the way round. If you do one thing here, read that fourth panel out loud to whoever you came with, then look back across the water at the city it was written for. That is the whole visit, and it is enough.
lincoln-memorial-steps:
The steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Stop here before you go up, because this particular stair is a place in its own right, and almost everyone climbs straight past it in a hurry to reach the statue. Slow down on the way. The steps are wide and they are steep, and the higher you go the more of the city opens behind you.

Eighteen steps down from the chamber, on the landing, there is an inscription cut into the granite: I have a dream. It is small and flush with the stone, worn smooth by shoes, and you have to be looking for it to find it. Martin Luther King junior stood on this spot on the twenty eighth of August nineteen sixty three and spoke to a quarter of a million people filling the ground from here to the Washington Monument, with Lincoln at his back and the century since emancipation in front of him. The engraving was added in two thousand and three. Most visitors walk straight over it. Stand on it instead, and look at what he was looking at.

Twenty four years earlier the contralto Marian Anderson sang here on Easter Sunday to seventy five thousand people, after the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her perform in Constitution Hall because she was black. Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from that organisation over it and helped arrange this instead. Anderson opened with My Country, Tis of Thee. King was ten years old and listening on the radio. Two moments, twenty four years apart, on the same stone, and you are standing on both of them.

So stand on the landing and turn around before you turn back. The view down the reflecting pool to the monument is the view from the lectern. On a still morning the water holds the whole length of it, the obelisk upside down all the way to the far end, and the ground where the crowd stood runs flat and green between. The reason this became the country's gathering place is right in front of you: it is the one spot in Washington where a very large number of people can see one person and hear them. The steps rise like seats in a theatre, the ground falls away, and the water carries sound. Stand a moment and picture it full, the crowd running back to the treeline, all of them facing this stone.

A practical word. This landing is the busiest photograph on the mall, so if you want the inscription without a queue, come early or come late, when the light is low and the crowds have thinned. The memorial never closes and the steps are lit at night. Watch your footing either way, because the stone is smooth and there is no rail down the middle. Then go up and read the walls. But do this first, on the landing, with your back to Lincoln and the whole reason for the place laid out in front of you. Stand where King stood for one quiet minute before you join the line moving up. That minute is the one you will remember.
air-and-space-museum:
The National Air and Space Museum. This is the one where the objects are the actual objects, not replicas, and that is worth keeping in mind as you walk. You are not looking at models of famous machines. You are looking at the machines. Go in knowing that, and the room changes.

Start by looking up, because the great flying things hang from the ceiling. The Wright Flyer here is the machine from Kitty Hawk, the one that flew on the seventeenth of December nineteen oh three for twelve seconds. Stand under it and take in how little there is to it, wood and wire and cloth, more kite than aircraft. The Spirit of St Louis is the aircraft Charles Lindbergh flew alone across the Atlantic in thirty three and a half hours in nineteen twenty seven, with no forward windscreen, because they put a fuel tank there instead and he used a periscope. Picture that. He crossed an ocean unable to see straight ahead.

The Apollo eleven command module Columbia is the capsule that carried three men to the moon and back and splashed down in the Pacific. You can see the scorch on it, the burn of coming home through the atmosphere. It is smaller than you expect, and three grown men rode it a quarter of a million miles. Nearby there is a piece of moon rock you are allowed to put your finger on, brought back by Apollo seventeen in nineteen seventy two and polished smooth by millions of hands since. It is about three point eight billion years old. Put your finger on it. There are not many things older than the planet you can touch, and this one sits at a low rail, unremarkable, with a line of people waiting their turn to press a fingertip to it and move on.

Here is the thing to carry out the door. Sixty eight years separate the Wright Flyer from the lunar module. One human lifetime, from a wood and canvas machine that flew the length of a passenger jet, to men walking on another world. Those two objects are in the same building, and the museum is arranged so you feel that. Walk from one to the other slowly and let the distance between them land.

A few practical notes. It is free, like all the Smithsonians, but timed entry passes are required and they are released online in advance. Get one before you come, because turning up without one at the door is how a good morning goes wrong. The planetarium and the flight simulators cost extra, so decide up front whether you want them and buy those separately. Two hours is the minimum here, and you could give it a whole day without trying. Come early if you can. The first entry of the day is the quietest, and standing alone under the Wright Flyer for a minute before the school groups arrive is worth setting an alarm for. If you take one thing away, let it be the walk between the Flyer and the moon capsule, one lifetime apart, both of them real, both of them in front of you.
national-gallery-of-art:
The National Gallery of Art. It is free, it is always free, and that was a condition rather than an accident. Andrew Mellon gave his collection and the money for the building to the nation in nineteen thirty seven on the terms that it would never carry his name and never charge admission, so that later collectors would not feel they were adding to one man's monument. It worked. Others gave, and the collection now runs from the thirteenth century to now. Walk in without paying and let that sink in for a second, because almost nothing else this good costs nothing.

Go to the West Building first. The one object to find there is Ginevra de Benci by Leonardo da Vinci. It is the only painting by Leonardo in the Americas, there are fewer than twenty in the world, and it is a portrait of a sixteen year old Florentine woman with a juniper bush behind her head, which is a pun on her name. She is small, and she is easy to walk past in a room of larger paintings, so slow down and look for her. The face is pale and cool and slightly unimpressed, and she has been looking at visitors like that for more than five hundred years.

Look closely, and then look at the back. The bottom of the panel was cut off at some point in its history, so her hands are missing. On the back, painted to be seen, is a wreath and the motto beauty adorns virtue. The gallery hangs it so you can walk around and read it, which most people never think to do. Do the small circle. It is the only Leonardo on the continent and you have it to yourself if you arrive early.

Then walk the underground concourse to the East Building, which is Ieoh Ming Pei's sharp geometry of triangles, with a Calder mobile turning slowly in the atrium and modern work upstairs. The two buildings could not be more different, and moving between them is half the pleasure. The moving walkway between them passes under a ceiling of light, which children like more than most of the art, and honestly it is a good moment for everyone. Let the walkway carry you and look up.

A few practical things. The Sculpture Garden outside has a fountain in summer and becomes an ice rink in winter, and there is jazz there on Friday evenings from May, which is one of the better free evenings in the city. Give yourself two hours in the West Building and one in the East, and there is no ticket to book, so you can come and go as the weather and your feet decide. On a hot afternoon the marble halls are cool and quiet, and the benches are deep and empty, which is a reason of its own to be here when your feet have had enough of the rest of the city. If you do one thing, stand with Ginevra for a full minute before the room fills. Everything else here is a gift. She is the one that will not be anywhere else you go.
arlington-national-cemetery:
Arlington National Cemetery. Six hundred and thirty nine acres, more than four hundred thousand graves, and about twenty five funerals still held here every weekday. This is an active cemetery, not a monument, and the rules of behaviour follow from that. You will pass services in progress. Give them room, lower your eyes, and let them be.

The land was Robert E Lee's home. His wife inherited it, and when Lee left to command the Confederate army the Union took the estate and, in eighteen sixty four, began burying the war dead in the rose garden beside the house, deliberately, so the family could never return to live there. They started with the ground closest to the front door. Walk the older sections and you feel it, the white stones stepping outward from the house in every direction, row after row, all the same size, arranged so no rank stands taller than another. Whichever way you turn, the lines of them close up and open again, and the ground is quiet enough that gravel underfoot is the loudest thing you hear.

Go to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. A sentinel from the Third Infantry Regiment has guarded it without pause since nineteen thirty seven, through hurricanes and blizzards and every night of every year. The routine is exact. Twenty one steps, a turn, twenty one seconds facing the tomb, and back, the count matching the twenty one gun salute. Watch it through once from the start of a cycle to the end, and watch the crowd rather than only the guard, because the whole plaza goes quiet on its own. The changing of the guard happens every hour in winter and every half hour in summer, and it is silent, apart from the heels on the stone and a single order given low. Stand still for it, and do not photograph over the heads of the people in front. Let it be what it is.

The Kennedy grave with its eternal flame is on the slope below Arlington House, and from that terrace you get the view down over the river to the Lincoln Memorial and the city. It is the one place in the cemetery where you can see what the graves face, and it is worth the climb to stand there for a moment before you turn back.

Practical and important. This is hilly and it is far larger than it looks, so wear real shoes or take the tram, which loops the main stops and saves your legs for the parts that matter. Bring water in summer, because the hills are exposed and the walk between the tomb and the Kennedy grave is longer than the map suggests. Give yourself at least two hours, and more if you have someone to find, and ask at the welcome centre for help locating a specific grave rather than searching the rows alone. Phones on silent, hats off at the tomb, and keep your voice low everywhere. This is not a place you tour so much as a place you are quiet in. Somebody is being buried here today. Walk softly, and when you leave, leave the way you would leave a service, without hurry and without noise.
